canonical-momentum-component-37776ef0.title: Generalized Canonical Momentum Component
canonical-momentum-component-37776ef0.description: Represents the $k$-th component of generalized canonical momentum conjugate to the generalized coordinate $q_k$ in Lagrangian and Hamiltonian mechanics.
canonical-momentum-component-37776ef0.conceptual_definition: The canonical momentum component $p_k$ is the dynamical variable conjugate to the generalized coordinate $q_k$, defined via the fiber derivative of the Lagrangian $L(q, \dot{q}, t)$ with respect to generalized velocity $\dot{q}_k$, giving $p_k = \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{q}_k}$. In the Hamiltonian formulation, $p_k$ serves as an independent coordinate spanning the $2n$-dimensional phase space manifold alongside $q_k$.
canonical-momentum-component-37776ef0.interpretation: The symbol $p_k$ designates the $k$-th component of the conjugate momentum vector. In simple Cartesian systems with velocity-independent potentials, $p_k$ reduces to the standard kinematic momentum $m \dot{x}_k$. In the presence of velocity-dependent potentials (such as electromagnetic interactions with vector potential $\mathbf{A}$), $p_k$ acquires an additional field term $q A_k$. If the Lagrangian possesses continuous translational symmetry along $q_k$ (such that $\frac{\partial L}{\partial q_k} = 0$), $p_k$ is a conserved Noether charge.
canonical-momentum-component-37776ef0.limits_and_boundary: In the non-relativistic, uncharged limit, $p_k \to m \dot{q}_k$. In quantum mechanics under canonical quantization, $p_k \to -i\hbar \frac{\partial}{\partial q_k}$, recovering the classical value in the macroscopic limit $\hbar \to 0$ via the correspondence principle.
canonical-momentum-component-37776ef0.symmetry_origin: Rooted in Noether's theorem via spatial translation and generalized cyclic coordinate invariance. If the Lagrangian is invariant under continuous shifts in $q_k$, the conjugate momentum $p_k$ is a strictly conserved constant of motion.

type-2-generating-function-momentum-rela.title: Type-2 Generating Function Momentum Relation
type-2-generating-function-momentum-rela.description: Expresses the original canonical momentum as the partial derivative of a Type-2 generating function with respect to the original generalized coordinate.
type-2-generating-function-momentum-rela.conceptual_definition: In canonical transformation theory within Hamiltonian mechanics, a Type-2 generating function $F_2(q, P, t)$ depends on the original generalized coordinates $q_i$, the transformed canonical momenta $P_i$, and optionally time $t$. The differential relation $dF_2 = p_i dq_i + Q_i dP_i + (K - H)dt$ directly implies that the original canonical momenta are given by $p_i = \frac{\partial F_2(q, P, t)}{\partial q_i}$, ensuring the preservation of the symplectic structure of phase space.
type-2-generating-function-momentum-rela.interpretation: In this relation, $p_i$ represents the $i$-th component of the original conjugate momentum, obtained by taking the partial derivative of the generating function $F_2(q, P, t)$ with respect to the original generalized coordinate $q_i$ while holding the new canonical momenta $P$ and time $t$ fixed. When $F_2$ is identified with Hamilton's principal function $S(q, P, t)$, this relation reproduces the fundamental momentum gradient equation of the Hamilton-Jacobi formalism.
type-2-generating-function-momentum-rela.limits_and_boundary: In the identity transformation where $F_2(q, P) = q_i P_i$, the relation trivially reduces to $p_i = P_i$. In the semiclassical limit $\hbar \to 0$, the quantum mechanical wave function phase gradient corresponds to this classical momentum-generating relation via the WKB approximation.
type-2-generating-function-momentum-rela.symmetry_origin: Rooted in the symplectic geometry of Hamiltonian phase space and the invariance of the canonical 1-form (Poincaré-Cartan integral invariant) under canonical transformations.

condition-for-momentum-conservation-acf2.title: Condition for Conservation of Total Linear Momentum
condition-for-momentum-conservation-acf2.description: States that the vanishing of the net external vector force acting on a physical system is the necessary and sufficient condition for the total linear momentum of the system to be conserved over time.
condition-for-momentum-conservation-acf2.conceptual_definition: In classical mechanics, the time rate of change of the total linear momentum $\mathbf{P}_{\text{total}}$ of a system of particles equals the vector sum of all external forces, $\mathbf{F}_{\text{ext}} = \frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{P}_{\text{total}}}{\mathrm{d}t}$. Consequently, the condition $\mathbf{F}_{\text{ext}} = 0$ implies that $\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{P}_{\text{total}}}{\mathrm{d}t} = 0$, establishing an isolated system whose total linear momentum remains temporally invariant.
condition-for-momentum-conservation-acf2.interpretation: The vector quantity $\mathbf{F}_{\text{ext}}$ denotes the net external force exerted on the system by external agents, defined as the vector sum $\sum_{i} \mathbf{F}_i^{(\text{ext})}$. When $\mathbf{F}_{\text{ext}} = 0$, internal pairwise interactions cancel identically due to Newton's third law in strong form ($\mathbf{F}_{ij} = -\mathbf{F}_{ji}$), ensuring that the velocity of the center of mass $\mathbf{v}_{\text{cm}}$ remains strictly constant.
condition-for-momentum-conservation-acf2.limits_and_boundary: In relativistic mechanics ($v \to c$), the condition extends to the four-force $K^\mu = 0$, ensuring the conservation of the four-momentum $P^\mu$. In quantum mechanics ($\hbar \neq 0$), the expectation value satisfies Ehrenfest's theorem $\frac{\mathrm{d}\langle \hat{\mathbf{P}} \rangle}{\mathrm{d}t} = \langle \hat{\mathbf{F}}_{\text{ext}} \rangle = 0$.
condition-for-momentum-conservation-acf2.symmetry_origin: Continuous spatial translation invariance of the Lagrangian or Hamiltonian via Noether's theorem, corresponding to homogeneity of space.

relativistic-lorentz-factor-48284763.title: Relativistic Lorentz Factor
relativistic-lorentz-factor-48284763.description: The Lorentz factor $\gamma$ is a fundamental scaling factor in special relativity that quantifies the kinematic modifications to time, length, and relativistic momentum for an object moving at speed $v$ relative to an inertial observer.
relativistic-lorentz-factor-48284763.conceptual_definition: The Lorentz factor $\gamma = (1 - v^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$ emerges directly from the invariance of the spacetime interval $ds^2 = c^2 dt^2 - d\mathbf{x}^2$ under Lorentz transformations in Minkowski spacetime. It establishes the hyperbolic angle (rapidity $\phi$) relationship $\gamma = \cosh\phi$ that maps inertial coordinate transformations between reference frames in relative motion.
relativistic-lorentz-factor-48284763.interpretation: In this equation, $\gamma$ represents the dimensionless Lorentz factor. The parameter $v$ is the magnitude of the relative velocity between two inertial frames of reference, and $c$ is the universal speed of light in vacuum. When $v = 0$, $\gamma = 1$, recovering classical Newtonian kinematics. For any non-zero speed $v < c$, $\gamma > 1$, scaling physical quantities such that moving clocks run slower by a factor of $\gamma$ (time dilation) and moving rods appear shortened by $1/\gamma$ along the direction of motion (length contraction).
relativistic-lorentz-factor-48284763.limits_and_boundary: In the non-relativistic limit $v/c \to 0$, $\gamma \to 1 + \frac{1}{2}\frac{v^2}{c^2} + \mathcal{O}(v^4/c^4) \to 1$, smoothly reducing to Galilean relativity. In the ultra-relativistic limit $v \to c$, $\gamma \to \infty$, preventing massive particles from reaching or exceeding the speed of light $c$.
relativistic-lorentz-factor-48284763.symmetry_origin: Global Lorentz invariance $\mathrm{SO}(1,3)$, expressing the isometry of flat Minkowski spacetime and the constancy of the speed of light in all inertial reference frames.

relativistic-lorentz-factor-48284763.intuitive_summary: As an object moves faster through space, its progression through coordinate time must adjust to ensure that the speed of light remains constant for all observers. The Lorentz factor measures this geometric scaling: negligible at everyday velocities, but diverging toward infinity as relative speed approaches the speed of light.

time-component-of-four-velocity-non-rela.title: Non-Relativistic Approximation of the Four-Velocity Temporal Component
time-component-of-four-velocity-non-rela.description: In the non-relativistic regime ($v \ll c$), the temporal component of the relativistic four-velocity $U^0 = \gamma c$ reduces asymptotically to the speed of light $c$ as the Lorentz factor $\gamma \to 1$.
time-component-of-four-velocity-non-rela.conceptual_definition: The contravariant four-velocity $U^\mu$ of a massive particle is defined as the derivative of its spacetime position $x^\mu = (ct, \mathbf{x})$ with respect to proper time $\tau$, yielding $U^0 = c \frac{dt}{d\tau} = \gamma c$. In the low-velocity limit where $v/c \to 0$, the Lorentz factor $\gamma = (1 - v^2/c^2)^{-1/2} \approx 1 + \frac{1}{2}\frac{v^2}{c^2} + \mathcal{O}(v^4/c^4)$, leading directly to the non-relativistic approximation $U^0 \approx c$.
time-component-of-four-velocity-non-rela.interpretation: The term $U^0$ represents the zeroth (temporal) component of the particle's four-velocity, measuring the rate of flow of coordinate time with respect to proper time scaled by $c$. The constant $c$ is the universal speed of light in vacuum. Under low spatial velocities ($v = |\mathbf{v}| \ll c$), proper time $\tau$ coincides with coordinate time $t$, rendering relativistic time dilation negligible and leaving $c$ as the dominant constant scaling factor.
time-component-of-four-velocity-non-rela.limits_and_boundary: In the static limit $v \to 0$, $U^0 = c$ holds exactly. In the relativistic limit $v \to c$, $\gamma \to \infty$, and the approximation breaks down completely as $U^0 \to \infty$.
time-component-of-four-velocity-non-rela.symmetry_origin: Lorentz symmetry $SO(1,3)$ of Minkowski spacetime, specifically preserving the invariant Minkowski norm $U_\mu U^\mu = -c^2$ (or $+c^2$ depending on the metric signature convention) under global spacetime translations and rotations.

When an object is almost stationary or moving much slower than light, nearly all of its motion through spacetime is directed along the temporal axis, rendering $U^0 \approx c$.

inverse-cubic-centimeter-unit-9704af3f.title: Inverse Cubic Centimeter Unit of Volumetric Number Density
inverse-cubic-centimeter-unit-9704af3f.description: Represents the derived CGS unit of inverse volume, commonly employed to quantify particle number density, volumetric concentration, and charge carrier densities in physical systems.
inverse-cubic-centimeter-unit-9704af3f.conceptual_definition: The inverse cubic centimeter, denoted $\text{cm}^{-3}$, is a derived unit representing the reciprocal of the volume of a cube with edge length $1\text{ cm} = 10^{-2}\text{ m}$. In dimensional analysis, it possesses dimensions of length to the negative third power, $[L^{-3}]$, and converts to SI units via $1\text{ cm}^{-3} = 10^{6}\text{ m}^{-3}$. It serves as the standard unit of volumetric number density $n = N/V$ in plasma physics, solid-state astrophysics, and chemistry.
inverse-cubic-centimeter-unit-9704af3f.interpretation: Physically, $\text{cm}^{-3}$ quantifies the concentration of discrete quanta or states per unit volume. For instance, the photon number density of the cosmic microwave background is approximately $n_\gamma \approx 411\text{ cm}^{-3}$, typical semiconductor intrinsic carrier densities $n_i$ are indexed in $\text{cm}^{-3}$, and interstellar medium particle densities range from $10^{-4}\text{ cm}^{-3}$ in the warm ionized medium to $10^{6}\text{ cm}^{-3}$ in dense molecular cores.
inverse-cubic-centimeter-unit-9704af3f.limits_and_boundary: In the continuum limit where sample volume $V \to \infty$ with constant particle number $N$, the local density approaches the thermodynamic limit $n = \lim_{V \to \infty} N/V$. At microscopic limits where the sampling volume approaches interparticle spacing $V \sim n^{-1}$, discrete statistical fluctuations become dominant.
inverse-cubic-centimeter-unit-9704af3f.symmetry_origin: Derived from the spatial translational and rotational invariance of 3D Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^3$, under which volume measures transform homogenously with scale factor $\lambda^3$ and reciprocal density measures transform as $\lambda^{-3}$.

perpendicular-component-of-acceleration-.title: Perpendicular Component of Acceleration Vector
perpendicular-component-of-acceleration-.description: The transverse or centripetal component of the three-acceleration vector oriented perpendicular to the instantaneous velocity vector.
perpendicular-component-of-acceleration-.conceptual_definition: The perpendicular acceleration $\mathbf{a}_\perp = \mathbf{a} - \frac{(\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{v})}{v^2}\mathbf{v} = \frac{\mathbf{v} \times (\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{v})}{v^2}$ quantifies the instantaneous rate of change in the direction of the velocity vector $\mathbf{v}$, defining the local trajectory curvature $\kappa = \frac{|\mathbf{a}_\perp|}{v^2}$ along the principal normal in the Frenet-Serret frame.
perpendicular-component-of-acceleration-.interpretation: The vector $\mathbf{a}_\perp$ represents the normal component of instantaneous acceleration $\mathbf{a}$. In classical mechanics, it corresponds to centripetal acceleration $\frac{v^2}{\rho}\hat{\mathbf{n}}$, where $\rho$ is the local radius of curvature and $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ is the principal unit normal. In relativistic electrodynamics, non-zero $\mathbf{a}_\perp$ produces synchrotron radiation proportional to $\gamma^4 |\mathbf{a}_\perp|^2$.
perpendicular-component-of-acceleration-.limits_and_boundary: In the rectilinear motion limit, $\mathbf{a} \parallel \mathbf{v}$, yielding $|\mathbf{a}_\perp| \to 0$. In uniform circular motion of radius $R$, $|\mathbf{a}_\perp| = \frac{v^2}{R}$ and $\mathbf{a}_\parallel = 0$. For relativistic speeds $v \to c$, radiation emission power is dominated by transverse acceleration scaling as $\gamma^4$.
perpendicular-component-of-acceleration-.symmetry_origin: Rotational invariance ($SO(3)$) of spatial coordinates and local geometric invariance of smooth curves parameterized by arc length in differential geometry.

\\mathbf{a}_\\perp.name: Perpendicular acceleration vector

perpendicular-component-of-acceleration-.intuitive_summary: While parallel acceleration changes an object's speed, perpendicular acceleration purely bends its direction of motion without changing speed.

inverse-square-radial-dependence-9078510.title: Inverse-Square Radial Scaling Factor
inverse-square-radial-dependence-9078510.description: Represents the standard geometric dilution factor $r^{-2}$ governing conserved flux and central potential gradients across three-dimensional Euclidean space.
inverse-square-radial-dependence-9078510.conceptual_definition: The mathematical factor $r^{-2}$ characterizes the falloff of fields and radiant intensity emitted isotropically from a point source in $(3+1)$-dimensional spacetime. It arises directly from Gauss's theorem applied to a two-sphere boundary $S^2$, where the surface area grows as $4\pi r^2$, thereby distributing a conserved total flux over an area proportional to the square of the radial coordinate $r$.
inverse-square-radial-dependence-9078510.interpretation: The term $r^{-2}$ quantifies radial attenuation. The radial coordinate $r$ measures the Euclidean distance from the origin or point source. When $r$ is scaled by a factor of $\alpha$, the corresponding quantity scales by $\alpha^{-2}$. In field theories and classical mechanics, $r^{-2}$ governs the gradient $-\nabla (1/r) = r^{-2} \hat{\mathbf{r}}$, giving rise to Coulomb and Newtonian force laws.
inverse-square-radial-dependence-9078510.limits_and_boundary: As $r \to 0$, $r^{-2} \to \infty$, representing a classical ultraviolet point singularity that requires regularization or quantum corrections. As $r \to \infty$, $r^{-2} \to 0$, enforcing asymptotic flatness and field decoupling at spatial infinity.
inverse-square-radial-dependence-9078510.symmetry_origin: Continuous spatial $SO(3)$ rotational symmetry and conservation of field flux via Gauss's divergence theorem in 3D Euclidean space.

inverse-square-radial-dependence-9078510.intuitive_summary: As energy, gravitational influence, or electric field spreads spherically outward from a source, the surface area over which it distributes grows as $r^2$, diluting the field's intensity by a factor of $1/r^2$.

stellar-composition-pure-heavy-elements-.title: Stellar Composition: Pure Heavy Elements (Metals)
stellar-composition-pure-heavy-elements-.description: Defines an extreme stellar chemical abundance profile where hydrogen and helium mass fractions vanish identically, leaving the stellar plasma comprised entirely of heavier elements ($Z = 1$).
stellar-composition-pure-heavy-elements-.conceptual_definition: In stellar astrophysics, the elemental composition of plasma is parameterized by the mass fractions $X$ (hydrogen), $Y$ (helium), and $Z$ (all elements heavier than helium, termed 'metals'), satisfying the normalization constraint $X + Y + Z = 1$. The state $X = 0, Y = 0, Z = 1$ denotes the limiting regime of complete hydrogen and helium depletion, typical of late-stage stellar cores (such as carbon-oxygen or iron cores in evolved massive stars) or exotic stripped stellar remnants.
stellar-composition-pure-heavy-elements-.interpretation: The condition $X = 0$ implies that no hydrogen nuclei ($^1\mathrm{H}$) remain to fuel pp-chain or CNO-cycle hydrogen burning. The condition $Y = 0$ indicates the absence of helium ($^4\mathrm{He}$), precluding triple-alpha fusion. Consequently, $Z = 1$ forces the entire mass fraction into heavy nuclides with atomic number $A_i \ge 12$, drastically elevating the mean molecular weight $\mu$ (with $\mu \approx 2$ for fully ionized heavy elements with $Z_i/A_i \approx 0.5$) and significantly altering the plasma equation of state, opacity, and electron degeneracy thresholds.
stellar-composition-pure-heavy-elements-.limits_and_boundary: In the limit $X \to 0$ and $Y \to 0$, the mean molecular weight for a fully ionized gas reaches its heavy-metal plateau $\mu^{-1} \approx \sum_i \frac{Z_i + 1}{A_i} Z_i \approx 0.5$, maximizing $\mu \approx 2.0$. This contrasts with pure ionized hydrogen where $\mu = 0.5$ and pure ionized helium where $\mu = 4/3$.
stellar-composition-pure-heavy-elements-.symmetry_origin: Baryon number conservation and total mass conservation enforce the fundamental normalization condition $\sum_i X_i = X + Y + Z = 1$.

canonical-action-integral-component-baa6.title: Canonical Action Integral along a Closed Path
canonical-action-integral-component-baa6.description: Represents the contour line integral of canonical momentum over a generalized coordinate for a complete periodic orbit, defining the phase space area enclosed by a cyclic trajectory.
canonical-action-integral-component-baa6.conceptual_definition: The canonical action integral $\oint p \, dq$ computes the abbreviated action or phase space area enclosed by a one-dimensional periodic or librational orbit in canonical coordinates $(q, p)$. It serves as the classical basis for action variables $J = \frac{1}{2\pi}\oint p \, dq$ in Hamiltonian mechanics and constitutes the foundation of the Wilson-Bohr-Sommerfeld quantization condition $\oint p \, dq = n h$ in old quantum theory.
canonical-action-integral-component-baa6.interpretation: The contour integral $\oint$ denotes integration along a closed trajectory $\gamma$ in the two-dimensional canonical phase space. Here, $p$ represents the generalized canonical momentum conjugate to the generalized coordinate $q$. By Green's theorem (or Stokes' theorem), $\oint p \, dq = \iint_{\Sigma} dp \wedge dq$, matching the symplectic 2-form area enclosed by the periodic trajectory $\partial \Sigma = \gamma$. Under slow variations of Hamiltonian parameters, this integral is an adiabatic invariant.
canonical-action-integral-component-baa6.limits_and_boundary: In the classical-to-quantum correspondence limit $\hbar \to 0$, the quantized phase space cells $\Delta q \Delta p \sim h$ form a continuum. For harmonic oscillation with energy $E$ and frequency $\omega$, the integral reduces to $\frac{2\pi E}{\omega}$. In the limit of open, unbound orbits ($E > V_{\infty}$), the path ceases to be closed and the integral diverges or transitions to an open line integral.
canonical-action-integral-component-baa6.symmetry_origin: Symplectic invariance under canonical transformations (preservation of the Poincaré-Cartan integral invariant $\oint \sum_i p_i \, dq_i - H \, dt$) and time-translation symmetry for autonomous conservative systems.

proper-time-differential-relation-11e8f2.title: Differential Proper Time Relation in Special Relativity
proper-time-differential-relation-11e8f2.description: Expresses the infinitesimal proper time interval $d\tau$ elapsed along a timelike worldline in terms of the coordinate time interval $dt$ and the Lorentz factor $\gamma$.
proper-time-differential-relation-11e8f2.conceptual_definition: In special relativity, proper time $\tau$ is the time measured by a clock traveling along a specific worldline. For a particle moving with instantaneous coordinate velocity $v = |\mathbf{v}|$ relative to an inertial reference frame, the infinitesimal proper time differential $d\tau$ is related to the coordinate time differential $dt$ through $d\tau = dt/\gamma$, where $\gamma = (1 - v^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$ is the relativistic Lorentz factor.
proper-time-differential-relation-11e8f2.interpretation: The equation $d\tau = dt/\gamma$ establishes that proper time $d\tau$ is an invariant quantity parameterizing timelike trajectories, directly proportional to the spacetime metric line element $ds/c$. The coordinate time differential $dt$ represents the time separation between two events as recorded by synchronized clocks at rest in the chosen inertial reference frame. The Lorentz factor $\gamma = (1 - v^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$ encapsulates relativistic kinematic time dilation, diverging as the instantaneous speed $v$ approaches the speed of light $c$.
proper-time-differential-relation-11e8f2.limits_and_boundary: In the non-relativistic limit $v/c \to 0$, the Lorentz factor $\gamma \to 1$, recovering classical absolute time $d\tau = dt$. In the ultra-relativistic limit $v \to c$, $\gamma \to \infty$, leading to $d\tau \to 0$, which signifies that massless particles (such as photons) experience zero proper time along null trajectories.
proper-time-differential-relation-11e8f2.symmetry_origin: Invariance of the spacetime interval under the Poincaré group (Lorentz transformations and spacetime translations), ensuring $c^2 d\tau^2 = c^2 dt^2 - d\mathbf{x}^2$ is a Lorentz scalar.

Because $\gamma \ge 1$, the elapsed proper time $d\tau$ registered on the moving observer's co-moving clock is strictly less than or equal to the coordinate time interval $dt$.

yukawa-exponential-decay-factor-c6c72282.title: Yukawa Exponential Decay Factor
yukawa-exponential-decay-factor-c6c72282.description: Spatial exponential attenuation factor characterizing the finite interaction range of massive scalar or vector boson exchange in quantum field theory.
yukawa-exponential-decay-factor-c6c72282.conceptual_definition:
The Yukawa exponential decay factor $e^{-mr}$ modulates static potentials mediated by massive exchange quanta. Arising as the spatial Green's function pole factor of the Klein-Gordon operator $(
abla^2 - m^2)$, it screens long-range Coulomb-like $1/r$ interactions beyond the Compton wavelength $\lambda_C = \hbar / (m c) = 1/m$ (in natural units $\hbar = c = 1$).
yukawa-exponential-decay-factor-c6c72282.interpretation: In the factor $e^{-mr}$, the variable $r$ denotes the spatial separation between interacting source currents, while $m$ represents the invariant mass of the mediating field quanta (expressed in inverse length units $\text{m}^{-1}$ where $\hbar = c = 1$). As $r$ exceeds the characteristic range $r_0 = 1/m$, the exponential suppression dominates over power-law geometric dispersion, establishing a strictly short-range nuclear or screened force.
yukawa-exponential-decay-factor-c6c72282.limits_and_boundary: In the massless limit $m \to 0$, $e^{-mr} \to 1$, restoring the long-range Coulomb potential. As $r \to 0$, $e^{-mr} \to 1$, leaving the short-distance singularity dominated by $1/r$. In the asymptotic limit $r \to \infty$, $e^{-mr} \to 0$ exponentially faster than any power law.
yukawa-exponential-decay-factor-c6c72282.symmetry_origin: Originates from $SO(3)$ spatial rotational invariance and the Lorentz invariant mass-shell dispersion relation $p^2 - m^2 = 0$ of relativistic field theory.

yukawa-exponential-decay-factor-c6c72282.intuitive_summary: Forces carried by massive particles cannot reach infinitely far; the exponential decay factor acts as a physical cutoff that rapidly snuffs out the interaction at distances larger than the mediator's Compton wavelength.

expectation-value-of-potential-energy-a9.title: Expectation Value of Potential Energy
expectation-value-of-potential-energy-a9.description: The quantum mechanical average or statistical mean of the potential energy operator evaluated over a given wave function or state distribution.
expectation-value-of-potential-energy-a9.conceptual_definition: The expectation value of potential energy $\langle V \rangle$ represents the statistical mean outcome of measuring the potential energy $\hat{V}(\mathbf{r})$ on an ensemble of identically prepared quantum systems in state $|\psi\rangle$. In the position representation, it is evaluated as the integral $\langle V \rangle = \int_{\mathbb{R}^3} \psi^*(\mathbf{r}) V(\mathbf{r}) \psi(\mathbf{r}) \, \mathrm{d}^3\mathbf{r} = \int_{\mathbb{R}^3} V(\mathbf{r}) |\psi(\mathbf{r})|^2 \, \mathrm{d}^3\mathbf{r}$.
expectation-value-of-potential-energy-a9.interpretation: The quantity $\langle V \rangle$ is the expected potential energy contribution to the total energy expectation value $\langle H \rangle = \langle T \rangle + \langle V \rangle$. Here, $V(\mathbf{r})$ represents the multiplicative potential energy operator acting on the spatial probability density $|\psi(\mathbf{r})|^2$. In bound states governed by homogeneous power-law potentials $V(r) \propto r^k$, the Virial Theorem establishes a rigid ratio $2\langle T \rangle = k\langle V \rangle$.
expectation-value-of-potential-energy-a9.limits_and_boundary: In the classical limit $\hbar \to 0$, the wave packet localizes to a delta distribution $\lim_{\hbar \to 0} |\psi(\mathbf{r})|^2 = \delta(\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{r}_c(t))$, yielding $\langle V \rangle \to V(\mathbf{r}_c(t))$. For unbounded states as $r \to \infty$ in vanishing asymptotic potentials $\lim_{r \to \infty} V(r) = 0$, the potential expectation value $\langle V \rangle \to 0$.
expectation-value-of-potential-energy-a9.symmetry_origin: Global phase invariance $U(1)$ of the quantum state ensures probability conservation, while spatial translation and rotational symmetries of the underlying potential $V(\mathbf{r})$ determine the conservation of linear and angular momentum expectation values via Ehrenfest's theorem.

quantum-mechanical-generator-scaling-fac.title: Quantum Mechanical Generator Scaling Factor
quantum-mechanical-generator-scaling-fac.description: The fundamental coupling constant $i/\hbar$ converts self-adjoint physical observables into anti-Hermitian generators of unitary symmetry transformations and time evolution.
quantum-mechanical-generator-scaling-fac.conceptual_definition: In quantum mechanics, continuous symmetry transformations such as space translations, rotations, and time evolution are represented by unitary operators of the form $\hat{U}(\theta) = \exp\left(-\frac{i}{\hbar} \theta \hat{G}\right)$, where $\hat{G}$ is a Hermitian operator representing an observable (such as linear momentum, angular momentum, or the Hamiltonian). The factor $\frac{i}{\hbar}$ is the dimensional and algebraic converter that maps a real, dimensionful physical quantity with dimensions of action into a dimensionless, skew-Hermitian Lie algebra generator.
quantum-mechanical-generator-scaling-fac.interpretation: The imaginary unit $i$ is essential for unitarity: exponentiating an anti-Hermitian operator $-\frac{i}{\hbar}\hat{G}$ yields a unitary operator $\hat{U}$, which ensures conservation of total probability $\langle \psi | \psi \rangle = 1$. The reduced Planck constant $\hbar$ has dimensions of action ($\text{J}\cdot\text{s}$); dividing the product of the continuous transformation parameter and the physical generator (whose product has dimensions of action) by $\hbar$ renders the argument in the exponential strictly dimensionless.
quantum-mechanical-generator-scaling-fac.limits_and_boundary: In the classical limit $\hbar \to 0$, quantum phases oscillate infinitely rapidly ($e^{iS/\hbar}$), leading via the stationary phase approximation to classical trajectories governed by the principle of least action, and the quantum commutator bracket $\frac{1}{i\hbar}[\hat{A}, \hat{B}]$ transitions directly to the classical Poisson bracket $\{A, B\}$.
quantum-mechanical-generator-scaling-fac.symmetry_origin: Rooted in Stone's theorem on one-parameter unitary groups and Noether's theorem in quantum mechanics, establishing a one-to-one correspondence between continuous symmetry groups (Lie groups) and Hermitian quantum observables (Lie algebra generators).

i.name: Imaginary unit
i.description: Fundamental mathematical constant satisfying $i^2 = -1$, required to form skew-Hermitian Lie algebra generators from Hermitian observables.

\\hbar.name: Reduced Planck constant
\\hbar.description: Fundamental quantum of action setting the physical scale for quantum phase evolution and non-commutativity.

quantum-mechanical-generator-scaling-fac.intuitive_summary: In quantum theory, physical observables are real and measurable (Hermitian), but continuous physical transformations must preserve probability amplitudes (unitary). Multiplying an observable by $i/\hbar$ converts it into a pure phase rotation rate, setting the quantum scale where classical conserved quantities generate physical motions.

squared-cosine-of-angle-theta-4b8ea372.title: Squared Cosine Angular Projection Term
squared-cosine-of-angle-theta-4b8ea372.description: Represents the square of the trigonometric cosine of an angle $\theta$, commonly appearing in quadratic projection laws, angular power distributions, and polarization intensity profiles.
squared-cosine-of-angle-theta-4b8ea372.conceptual_definition: The expression $\cos^2 \theta$ quantifies the quadratic projection of a vector onto a reference axis or the squared overlap between two directional states. In physics, it underpins Malus's law for polarized light intensity $I = I_0 \cos^2 \theta$, dipolar radiation patterns, and quantum state transition probabilities $|⟨ \psi | \phi ⟩|^2$ between angular momentum states.
squared-cosine-of-angle-theta-4b8ea372.interpretation: The term $\cos^2 \theta$ provides an even, non-negative modulation bounded strictly in the interval $[0, 1]$. When $\theta = 0$ or $\theta = \pi$, the alignment is maximal ($\cos^2 \theta = 1$), corresponding to parallel or antiparallel orientation. When $\theta = \pi/2$ or $\theta = 3\pi/2$, the orientation is perpendicular, yielding $\cos^2 \theta = 0$. In electrodynamics and wave optics, this quadratic dependence naturally arises because physical intensities and energy densities scale quadratically with field amplitudes $\mathbf{E} \propto \cos \theta$.
squared-cosine-of-angle-theta-4b8ea372.limits_and_boundary: At $\theta \to 0$, $\cos^2 \theta \approx 1 - \theta^2 + \mathcal{O}(\theta^4)$. At $\theta = \pi/2$, $\cos^2 \theta = 0$. For any real angle $\theta \in \mathbb{R}$, $0 \le \cos^2 \theta \le 1$.
squared-cosine-of-angle-theta-4b8ea372.symmetry_origin: Invariance under parity and angle inversion $\theta \to -\theta$ and periodic reflection $\theta \to \theta + \pi$, reflecting parity-even ($P$-even) geometric alignment invariant to directional sense.

\\theta.description: Angle of orientation, displacement, or polarization relative to the reference axis

squared-cosine-of-angle-theta-4b8ea372.intuitive_summary: Measures the fraction of transmitted intensity or power as a function of alignment angle, peaking at full alignment or anti-alignment and vanishing when orthogonal.

temperature-weighted-second-entropy-vari.title: Temperature-Weighted Entropy Variation
temperature-weighted-second-entropy-vari.description: Represents the thermal energy contribution associated with variations in entropy, characterizing thermal fluctuations and thermodynamic stability criteria near equilibrium.
temperature-weighted-second-entropy-vari.conceptual_definition: The expression $T \delta S$ quantifies the infinitesimal quasi-static thermal heat transfer or energetic response induced by a perturbation in the entropy $\delta S$ at absolute equilibrium temperature $T$. In fluctuation theory and black hole thermodynamics, higher-order or perturbed contributions of the form $T \delta S$ enter into the expansion of the internal energy or mass functional to determine local thermodynamic stability.
temperature-weighted-second-entropy-vari.interpretation: The term $T \delta S$ represents the product of the intensive thermodynamic temperature $T$ and the extensive entropy variation $\delta S$. In stability analyses and the first law of thermodynamics, $\delta Q_{\mathrm{rev}} = T \delta S$ corresponds to the reversible heat exchange. In second-order perturbation theory of thermodynamic potentials, sign definiteness of variations weighted by $T$ governs the convexity of entropy and thermodynamic stability against fluctuations.
temperature-weighted-second-entropy-vari.limits_and_boundary: In the limit $T \to 0$, $T \delta S \to 0$ in accordance with the Third Law of Thermodynamics (Nernst Heat Theorem), as entropic fluctuations become energetically suppressed. For $\delta S \to 0$, the variation vanishes, characterizing an unperturbed equilibrium state.
temperature-weighted-second-entropy-vari.symmetry_origin: Time-translation invariance governing energy conservation via Noether's theorem, combined with maximum entropy principles arising from statistical phase-space volume maximization.

T.name: Absolute Temperature
T.description: Thermodynamic equilibrium temperature defining the thermal state of the system.

\\delta S.description: Perturbative variation or virtual change in the extensive entropy of the system.

temperature-weighted-second-entropy-vari.intuitive_summary: Multiplying an entropy change by the local temperature converts dimensionless or information-theoretic entropy variations directly into physical units of energy, indicating how much thermal energy is absorbed, released, or redistributed during a perturbation.

orbital-angular-momentum-eigenvalue-fact.title: Orbital Angular Momentum Eigenvalue Factor
orbital-angular-momentum-eigenvalue-fact.description: The dimensionless quadratic Casimir eigenvalue factor $l(l+1)$ that parameterizes the spectrum of the squared orbital angular momentum operator $\hat{\mathbf{L}}^2$ in quantum mechanics.
orbital-angular-momentum-eigenvalue-fact.conceptual_definition: In the quantum mechanics of central potentials and rotational kinematics, the dimensionless eigenvalue factor $l(l+1)$ arises from the representation theory of the rotation group $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ and its Lie algebra $\mathfrak{so}(3)$. When the squared orbital angular momentum operator $\hat{\mathbf{L}}^2$ acts on spherical harmonics $Y_l^m(\theta, \phi)$, the resulting eigenvalue is $\hbar^2 l(l+1)$, where $l \in \{0, 1, 2, \dots\}$ is the azimuthal or orbital angular momentum quantum number.
orbital-angular-momentum-eigenvalue-fact.interpretation: The symbol $l$ represents the orbital angular momentum quantum number, restricted to non-negative integers $l \in \{0, 1, 2, \dots\}$ due to single-valuedness boundary conditions on the spherical wavefunction over the sphere $S^2$. The expression $l(l+1)$ scales the squared scale factor $\hbar^2$ to produce the total magnitude squared of the orbital angular momentum observable.
orbital-angular-momentum-eigenvalue-fact.limits_and_boundary: For the ground s-wave state ($l = 0$), the factor evaluates to $0(0+1) = 0$, yielding a spherically symmetric state with zero orbital angular momentum. In the semiclassical correspondence limit ($l \gg 1$), $l(l+1) = l^2(1 + 1/l) \approx l^2$, recovering classical continuous angular momentum scaling.
orbital-angular-momentum-eigenvalue-fact.symmetry_origin: Originates from the continuous rotational invariance of three-dimensional isotropic space under the Lie group $\mathrm{SO}(3)$. The operator $\hat{\mathbf{L}}^2$ is the quadratic Casimir invariant of the $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ Lie algebra, commuting with all generator components $[\hat{\mathbf{L}}^2, \hat{L}_i] = 0$.

l.name: orbital angular momentum quantum number
l.description: Azimuthal quantum number specifying the quantized rotational subshell and magnitude of orbital angular momentum

orbital-angular-momentum-eigenvalue-fact.intuitive_summary: In classical mechanics, the squared angular momentum is simply $L^2$. In quantum mechanics, quantum fluctuations and the non-commutativity of orthogonal angular momentum components $(\hat{L}_x, \hat{L}_y, \hat{L}_z)$ prevent total alignment along any single axis, adding an extra quantum correction $+l$ such that the magnitude scales as $l(l+1) = l^2 + l$ rather than $l^2$.

cylindrical-azimuthal-unit-vector-69863b.title: Cylindrical Azimuthal Unit Vector
cylindrical-azimuthal-unit-vector-69863b.description: The normalized basis vector pointing in the direction of increasing azimuthal angle in a cylindrical coordinate system.
cylindrical-azimuthal-unit-vector-69863b.conceptual_definition: In cylindrical coordinates $(s, \phi, z)$ defined by Cartesian mappings $x = s\cos\phi$, $y = s\sin\phi$, and $z = z$, the azimuthal unit vector $\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}$ is defined geometrically as the tangent unit vector to coordinate curves of constant $s$ and $z$: $\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}} = \frac{1}{s} \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}}{\partial \phi} = -\sin\phi \,\hat{\mathbf{i}} + \cos\phi \,\hat{\mathbf{j}}$.
cylindrical-azimuthal-unit-vector-69863b.interpretation: The unit vector $\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}$ forms an orthonormal basis with the radial unit vector $\hat{\mathbf{s}}$ and the axial unit vector $\hat{\mathbf{z}}$, satisfying $\hat{\mathbf{s}} \times \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}} = \hat{\mathbf{z}}$. Unlike Cartesian basis vectors, $\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}$ depends explicitly on the coordinate $\phi$, yielding non-zero spatial derivatives such as $\frac{\partial \hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}}{\partial \phi} = -\hat{\mathbf{s}}$, which generates centripetal and Coriolis acceleration terms in rotating frames.
cylindrical-azimuthal-unit-vector-69863b.limits_and_boundary: At the coordinate singularity on the $z$-axis ($s \to 0$), the azimuthal angle $\phi$ and hence $\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}$ become undefined. As $s \to \infty$, $\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}$ remains a well-defined local unit vector with invariant norm $\|\hat{\boldsymbol{\phi}}\| = 1$.
cylindrical-azimuthal-unit-vector-69863b.symmetry_origin: Originates from continuous planar rotational symmetry $SO(2)$ around the $z$-axis, acting as the normalized generator of azimuthal angular displacements.

\\hat{\\boldsymbol{\\phi}}.name: azimuthal unit vector
\\hat{\\boldsymbol{\\phi}}.description: Dimensionless unit basis vector pointing in the direction of increasing azimuthal angle $\phi$ in cylindrical coordinates.

cylindrical-azimuthal-unit-vector-69863b.intuitive_summary: The azimuthal unit vector points tangentially along concentric circles centered on the $z$-axis, indicating the direction of counterclockwise rotation in the transverse plane.

virtual-displacement-in-generalized-coor.title: Virtual Displacement in Generalized Coordinates
virtual-displacement-in-generalized-coor.description: Expresses the infinitesimal virtual displacement of the position vector of a particle in terms of arbitrary variations in the system's generalized coordinates at a frozen instant of time.
virtual-displacement-in-generalized-coor.conceptual_definition: A virtual displacement $\delta \mathbf{r}_i$ is an infinitesimal, kinematically admissible change in the configuration coordinates of the $i$-th particle consistent with the geometric constraints at fixed time ($t = \text{const.}$, hence $\delta t = 0$). By expanding the holonomic transformation relation $\mathbf{r}_i = \mathbf{r}_i(q_1, q_2, \dots, q_n, t)$, the virtual displacement in physical 3D space is obtained as the linear combination $\delta \mathbf{r}_i = \sum_j \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}_i}{\partial q_j} \delta q_j$, where the tangent vectors $\frac{\partial \mathbf{r}_i}{\partial q_j}$ span the tangent space to the configuration manifold.
virtual-displacement-in-generalized-coor.interpretation: The symbol $\delta \mathbf{r}_i$ represents the virtual displacement vector of the $i$-th particle. The generalized coordinates are given by $q_j$, with independent virtual variations $\delta q_j$. The partial derivative $\frac{\partial \mathbf{r}_i}{\partial q_j}$ represents the local coordinate basis vector or Jacobian coefficient that maps a displacement along the generalized coordinate $q_j$ into real Cartesian space.
virtual-displacement-in-generalized-coor.limits_and_boundary: For unconstrained Cartesian coordinates, $q_j = (x_i, y_i, z_i)$, leading to $\frac{\partial \mathbf{r}_i}{\partial q_j} = \mathbf{e}_j$ and $\delta \mathbf{r}_i = (\delta x_i, \delta y_i, \delta z_i)$. relative-measurement-angle-0976495e.title: Relative Measurement Angle in Bell Tests
relative-measurement-angle-0976495e.description: Quantifies the relative angular separation between two spatial detector orientations or polarization analyzer axes in quantum entanglement and Bell inequality experiments.
relative-measurement-angle-0976495e.conceptual_definition: The relative measurement angle $\theta_{ab}$ defines the geometric angle between the unit measurement vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ chosen by two spatially separated observers (traditionally Alice and Bob). For bipartite quantum systems such as spin-$1/2$ pairs or entangled photon polarizations, the quantum correlation expectation value $E(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}) = \langle (\boldsymbol{\sigma} \cdot \mathbf{a}) \otimes (\boldsymbol{\sigma} \cdot \mathbf{b}) \rangle$ evaluates as a function of this relative angle, typically $-\cos(\theta_{ab})$ for the singlet state $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(|01\rangle - |10\rangle)$ or $-\cos(2\theta_{ab})$ for photon polarization states.
relative-measurement-angle-0976495e.interpretation: The parameter $\theta_{ab}$ represents the interior angle satisfying $\cos(\theta_{ab}) = \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}$ between analyzer settings $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$. When $\theta_{ab} = 0$, measurement settings are aligned, yielding maximally anti-correlated (or correlated) outcomes for maximally entangled states. When $\theta_{ab} = \pi/2$, the measurement bases are mutually unbiased, resulting in zero statistical correlation $E(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}) = 0$.
relative-measurement-angle-0976495e.limits_and_boundary: As $\theta_{ab} \to 0$, the correlation reaches its extreme value $E = -1$ (perfect anti-correlation for singlet states). As $\theta_{ab} \to \pi/2$, measurements are orthogonal and statistically independent ($E = 0$). As $\theta_{ab} \to \pi$, the correlation flips sign to $E = +1$. Maximum violation of the CHSH Bell inequality occurs at settings where $\theta_{ab} = \pi/4$ and $3\pi/4$.
relative-measurement-angle-0976495e.symmetry_origin: Rotational invariance ($SO(3)$ or $SO(2)$ global spatial symmetry) of isotropic entangled states (e.g., the singlet state), ensuring quantum correlation depends solely on the relative scalar product $\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = \cos(\theta_{ab})$.

linear-momentum-definition-a617aed8.title: Classical Linear Momentum Definition
linear-momentum-definition-a617aed8.description: Defines the non-relativistic linear momentum vector of a point particle as the product of its invariant inertial mass and instantaneous velocity vector.
linear-momentum-definition-a617aed8.conceptual_definition: In Newtonian mechanics, linear momentum $\boldsymbol{p}$ quantifies the translational quantity of motion of a body. Defined as $\boldsymbol{p} = m\boldsymbol{v}$, it represents the vector generator of spatial translations and acts as the fundamental dynamical quantity appearing in Newton's second law, $\mathbf{F} = \frac{\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{p}}{\mathrm{d}t}$.
linear-momentum-definition-a617aed8.interpretation: The vector $\boldsymbol{p}$ is collinear with the velocity vector $\boldsymbol{v}$ and scales linearly with the scalar inertial mass $m$. Because $m > 0$, momentum shares the identical directional orientation as the instantaneous displacement rate $\boldsymbol{v} = \frac{\mathrm{d}\boldsymbol{r}}{\mathrm{d}t}$. In an isolated system without external forces, the total linear momentum is strictly conserved across all interactions.
linear-momentum-definition-a617aed8.limits_and_boundary: Valid exclusively in the non-relativistic regime where particle speed satisfies $v \ll c$. In the ultra-relativistic limit $v \to c$, the definition breaks down and must be replaced by relativistic momentum $\boldsymbol{p} = \gamma m_0 \boldsymbol{v}$, where $\gamma = (1 - v^2/c^2)^{-1/2}$.
linear-momentum-definition-a617aed8.symmetry_origin: Continuous spatial translation invariance of the Lagrangian via Noether's theorem leads directly to the conservation of linear momentum.

exchange-coupling-constant-d6938b7c.title: Exchange Coupling Constant

In the limit $J_{ij} = 0$, the magnetic interaction between sites $i$ and $j$ vanishes, leaving the spins decoupled.

principle-of-stationary-action-73fb895c.title: Hamilton's Principle of Stationary Action
principle-of-stationary-action-73fb895c.description: States that the true trajectory traversed by a physical system between fixed initial and final configurations makes the action functional stationary under arbitrary first-order variations.
principle-of-stationary-action-73fb895c.conceptual_definition: Hamilton's principle asserts that the classical evolution of a dynamic system described by generalized coordinates $\{q_i(t)\}$ between fixed endpoints $q_i(t_1)$ and $q_i(t_2)$ extremizes the action functional $S = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} L(q, \dot{q}, t) \, dt$. The integrand $L = T - V$ is the system Lagrangian representing the difference between kinetic energy $T$ and potential energy $V$. The parameter $t$ is the independent time variable. mass-ratio-of-particle-2-to-total-mass-1.description: This component represents the ratio of the mass of particle 2 to the total mass of a two-particle system. It acts as a weighting factor in center-of-mass frame transformations.
mass-ratio-of-particle-2-to-total-mass-1.conceptual_definition: In a two-body system, this dimensionless ratio quantifies the relative contribution of particle 2's mass to the system's overall mass. mass-ratio-of-particle-2-to-total-mass-1.interpretation: The ratio $\frac{m_2}{M}$ serves as a scaling factor that determines how much the relative velocity of the two particles contributes to the individual velocity of particle 1 in the center-of-mass frame. A larger value of this ratio implies that particle 2 constitutes a significant portion of the total mass, meaning particle 1 is comparatively lighter and its motion is more strongly influenced by the relative motion. Conversely, if $m_2$ is much smaller than $M$ (implying $m_1$ is dominant), this ratio approaches zero, indicating that particle 1's velocity is primarily dictated by the center-of-mass velocity, with minimal impact from the relative motion.
mass-ratio-of-particle-2-to-total-mass-1.limits_and_boundary: The mass ratio $\frac{m_2}{M}$ is always a positive value between 0 and 1, exclusive. mass-ratio-of-particle-2-to-total-mass-1.symmetry_origin: This ratio itself does not directly represent a symmetry or conservation law. number-operator-definition-c874f608.conceptual_definition: The number operator $\hat{N} = a^\dagger a$ is an observable on Fock space that counts the occupation number of quanta in a specific quantum mode. Acting on an eigenstate (Fock state) $|n\rangle$, it returns the eigenvalue $n \in \mathbb{N}_0$ via the eigenvalue equation $\hat{N}|n\rangle = n|n\rangle$.
number-operator-definition-c874f608.interpretation: The operator $\hat{N}$ is a positive semi-definite, self-adjoint operator on the Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$. The operator $a$ represents the annihilation (or lowering) operator, which removes an excitation, while $a^\dagger$ represents the creation (or adjoint raising) operator. In a bosonic algebra where $[a, a^\dagger] = 1$, the operator $\hat{N}$ has spectrum $\{0, 1, 2, \dots\}$, whereas for fermions with $\{a, a^\dagger\} = 1$, the Pauli exclusion principle restricts eigenvalues to $\{0, 1\}$.
number-operator-definition-c874f608.limits_and_boundary: In the ground state $|0\rangle$, the expectation value vanishes identically: $\langle 0 | \hat{N} | 0 \rangle = 0$. In the classical limit $\hbar \to 0$ or high-excitation limit $n \gg 1$, quantum fluctuations become negligible relative to the total number, satisfying $\Delta N / \langle \hat{N} \rangle \to 0$ for coherent states.
number-operator-definition-c874f608.symmetry_origin: The conservation of the number operator $\hat{N}$ arises from global $U(1)$ phase invariance $\psi \to e^{i\alpha}\psi$ via Noether's theorem, corresponding to total particle or charge conservation.

electric-potential-difference-condition-.title: Electric Potential Gradient Inequality Condition
electric-potential-difference-condition-.description: An inequality specifying that the electrostatic scalar potential at position $B$ is strictly greater than at position $A$, establishing the direction of the mean electrostatic field along any connecting path.
electric-potential-difference-condition-.conceptual_definition: The condition $\Phi_B > \Phi_A$ denotes a positive electrostatic potential difference $\Delta \Phi = \Phi_B - \Phi_A > 0$ between two spatial points $A$ and $B$. In a conservative electrostatic field $\mathbf{E} = -\nabla \Phi$, this inequality corresponds to the path integral condition $-\int_A^B \mathbf{E} \cdot d\mathbf{l} > 0$, implying that the line integral of the electric field along a path from $A$ to $B$ is negative ($\int_A^B \mathbf{E} \cdot d\mathbf{l} < 0$). Consequently, moving a positive test charge $q > 0$ quasi-statically from $A$ to $B$ requires positive work from an external agent.
electric-potential-difference-condition-.interpretation: In this inequality, $\Phi_A$ represents the electrostatic potential evaluated at the spatial coordinate $\mathbf{r}_A$, and $\Phi_B$ is the potential at $\mathbf{r}_B$. The strict inequality $\Phi_B > \Phi_A$ dictates that the conservative electric field $\mathbf{E}$ points preferentially from $B$ toward $A$. A free positive test charge ($q > 0$) naturally accelerates down the potential gradient from $B$ to $A$, converting electrostatic potential energy $\Delta U = q(\Phi_B - \Phi_A) > 0$ into kinetic energy.
electric-potential-difference-condition-.limits_and_boundary: In the infinitesimal spatial separation limit $|\mathbf{r}_B - \mathbf{r}_A| \to 0$, the finite difference condition $\Phi_B - \Phi_A > 0$ contracts to the directional derivative condition $\nabla \Phi \cdot d\mathbf{r} > 0$, or equivalently $\mathbf{E} \cdot d\mathbf{r} < 0$. If point $A$ is taken to spatial infinity with the standard boundary convention $\lim_{|\mathbf{r}| \to \infty} \Phi(\mathbf{r}) = 0$, the condition reduces to $\Phi_B > 0$.
electric-potential-difference-condition-.symmetry_origin: Electrostatic gauge invariance under the global transformation $\Phi(\mathbf{r}) \to \Phi(\mathbf{r}) + C$ preserves the inequality $\Phi_B > \Phi_A$ unchanged, as physical observables depend strictly on gauge-invariant potential differences $\Delta \Phi$.

wave-equation-for-electromagnetic-four-p.title: Wave Equation for Electromagnetic Four-Potential
wave-equation-for-electromagnetic-four-p.description: This equation describes the propagation of the electromagnetic four-potential in the presence of a four-current density, under the Lorenz gauge condition.
wave-equation-for-electromagnetic-four-p.conceptual_definition: This is the inhomogeneous wave equation for the electromagnetic four-potential $A^ u$, which combines the scalar potential and vector potential into a single relativistic four-vector. It is a direct consequence of Maxwell's equations when expressed in terms of potentials and subject to the Lorenz gauge condition. The equation demonstrates how electromagnetic waves are generated and propagate from charge and current distributions.
wave-equation-for-electromagnetic-four-p.interpretation: The left side, $\square A^ u$, represents the d'Alembertian operator acting on the four-potential, indicating wave-like propagation through spacetime. The right side, $\mu_0 J^ u$, signifies that the four-current density $J^ u$ acts as the source for these electromagnetic waves. This equation unifies the description of electric and magnetic fields, showing that they are components of a single electromagnetic field tensor derived from $A^ u$, and that their dynamics are governed by the distribution and motion of charges and currents. It is a fundamental equation in relativistic electrodynamics.
wave-equation-for-electromagnetic-four-p.limits_and_boundary: This equation is valid in the context of classical electrodynamics and special relativity. It specifically holds true when the electromagnetic potentials satisfy the Lorenz gauge condition, $\partial_\mu A^\mu = 0$. It describes fields in a vacuum or linear, isotropic, homogeneous media where $\mu_0$ can be replaced by the medium's permeability. It does not account for quantum effects or strong gravitational fields.
wave-equation-for-electromagnetic-four-p.symmetry_origin: The equation is manifestly Lorentz covariant, meaning its form is invariant under Lorentz transformations, reflecting the principles of special relativity. Its derivation relies on the freedom to choose a gauge for the electromagnetic potentials, specifically fixing it to the Lorenz gauge, which itself is a Lorentz-invariant condition. This gauge choice simplifies Maxwell's equations into these wave equations.

\\square.name: \square
\\square.description: The d'Alembertian operator, defined as $\frac{1}{c^2}\frac{\partial^2}{\partial t^2} - \nabla^2$ in SI units, where $c$ is the speed of light in vacuum. It represents the wave operator in four-dimensional spacetime. Units: $m^{-2}$.

A^\\nu.name: A^\nu
A^\\nu.description: The electromagnetic four-potential, a four-vector combining the scalar potential $\phi$ and the vector potential $\mathbf{A}$ as $A^\nu = (\phi/c, \mathbf{A})$. It describes the electromagnetic field. Units: $V \cdot s \cdot m^{-1}$.

\\mu_0.name: \mu_0
\\mu_0.description: The permeability of free space, a fundamental physical constant. It relates magnetic fields to electric currents. Units: $N \cdot A^{-2}$ or $H \cdot m^{-1}$.

J^\\nu.name: J^\nu
J^\\nu.description: The four-current density, a four-vector combining the charge density $\rho$ and the current density $\mathbf{J}$ as $J^\nu = (c\rho, \mathbf{J})$. It represents the source of the electromagnetic field. Units: $A \cdot m^{-2}$.

potential-distance-power-law-ca419485.title: Potential-Distance Power Law
potential-distance-power-law-ca419485.description: This equation describes how a physical potential scales proportionally to a power of the distance from its source.
potential-distance-power-law-ca419485.conceptual_definition: In physics, a potential ( $V$) represents the potential energy per unit charge or mass at a given point in a field. This equation states that the potential's magnitude is directly proportional to the distance (r) raised to some power (n). This power law dependence is characteristic of many fundamental forces and fields, such as gravitational and electrostatic potentials.
potential-distance-power-law-ca419485.interpretation: The proportionality V $\propto$ r^n signifies that as the distance from the source changes, the potential changes in a predictable, non-linear fashion determined by the exponent $n$. For instance, in Newtonian gravity, the gravitational potential of a point mass is proportional to r^{-1} (i.e., n=-1). In electrostatics, the electric potential of a point charge is also proportional to r^{-1}. Different values of $n$ correspond to different physical scenarios or types of interactions, often reflecting the dimensionality of space or the nature of the source.
potential-distance-power-law-ca419485.limits_and_boundary: This power law relationship is typically valid for potentials generated by point sources or spherically symmetric distributions in an infinite, homogeneous medium. It may break down at very short distances (e.g., inside the source distribution) or very large distances where other effects (like screening or boundary conditions) become significant. The exponent $n$ is usually an integer or half-integer, determined by the specific physical law governing the potential.
potential-distance-power-law-ca419485.symmetry_origin: The inverse square law nature of fundamental forces (like gravity and electromagnetism) often leads to potentials that scale as r^{-1}. This inverse square dependence is a direct consequence of the spherical symmetry of the source and the three-dimensional nature of space, implying that the flux of the field spreads out over a surface area proportional to r^2.

V.name: V
V.description: Potential (e.g., electric potential in Volts (V) or gravitational potential in Joules per kilogram (J/kg))

n.name: n
n.description: Dimensionless exponent, determining the power-law dependence of the potential on distance

observed-counts-with-detection-inefficie.title: Observed Counts with Detection Inefficiency
observed-counts-with-detection-inefficie.description: This equation relates the observed number of events to the true number of events, accounting for a constant detection inefficiency or loss rate.
observed-counts-with-detection-inefficie.conceptual_definition: This equation models the relationship between the observed number of events and the true number of events, accounting for a constant detection inefficiency. It represents a simplified, linear model where a constant fraction of true events are systematically missed due to instrumental limitations.
observed-counts-with-detection-inefficie.interpretation: This formula states that the number of observed events, $N_{\mathrm{obs}}$, is directly proportional to the true number of events, $N_{\mathrm{true}}$, scaled by a factor representing the detection efficiency. The term $(1 - \epsilon)$ is the probability of detecting a single event, where $\epsilon$ is the inefficiency or loss rate. If $\epsilon = 0$, all true events are observed, implying perfect detection. If $\epsilon = 1$, no true events are observed, indicating complete detection failure. This is a fundamental concept in experimental data analysis, crucial for correcting raw measurements to infer underlying physical quantities.
observed-counts-with-detection-inefficie.limits_and_boundary:
The inefficiency parameter $\epsilon$ must be in the range $[0, 1]$.
If $\epsilon \to 0$, then $N_{\mathrm{obs}} \to N_{\mathrm{true}}$, representing perfect detection.
If $\epsilon \to 1$, then $N_{\mathrm{obs}} = 0$, representing complete detection failure.
Both $N_{\mathrm{obs}}$ and $N_{\mathrm{true}}$ are non-negative integers, as they represent counts of discrete events.
observed-counts-with-detection-inefficie.symmetry_origin: This formula does not directly arise from fundamental physical symmetries or conservation laws. It is an empirical or statistical relationship describing the performance of a measurement instrument. It implicitly assumes that the detection inefficiency is uniform and independent for each true event.

N_{\\mathrm{obs}}.name: Observed Counts
N_{\\mathrm{obs}}.description: The number of events or particles detected by an instrument, representing the raw count obtained from measurements.

N_{\\mathrm{true}}.name: True Counts
N_{\\mathrm{true}}.description: The true, underlying number of events or particles that occurred before any detection losses.

\\epsilon.name: Detection Inefficiency
\\epsilon.description: The fraction of true events that are not detected, a dimensionless quantity between 0 and 1.

observed-counts-with-detection-inefficie.intuitive_summary: The number of events you actually count is the true number of events minus a fraction lost due to your detector not being perfect.
